name: Identifiable Victim Effect
description: People often feel a stronger urge to help when harm is attached to one concrete, identified person than when the same harm is described statistically or spread across a group. A face, name, or single story can outweigh larger but abstract suffering.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to fundraising flows, crisis banners, trust-and-safety appeals, civic-service communication, and research storytelling: concrete individual cases can drive action more strongly than population summaries, even when the aggregate stakes are larger.
myth_risk_note: Lee & Feeley's (2016) meta-analysis across 41 studies reports a modest overall effect (r = .05), reliable mainly for a single identified victim under specific framings; Ein-Gar & Levontin (2012) show the effect can reverse under temporal/social distance -- real boundary conditions rather than a universal design principle.
prevalence_note: A recurring named idea in fundraising, cause communication, and public-interest design, but much less central in everyday SaaS/product UX critique than anchors, defaults, or social proof.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of 41 studies found the identifiable victim effect is real but modest overall (r=.05), reliable mainly under specific conditions: a single identified or single unidentified victim, a photographed child suffering from poverty, low attributed responsibility for the need, and/or a monetary request framing. An honest, effect-size-calibrated confirmation rather than a sweeping universal claim -- the popular framing of this effect as a powerful, general persuasion lever is real but genuinely narrower and weaker than commonly assumed.
findings.source_title: The identifiable victim effect: a meta-analytic review

findings.description: Across helping-choice experiments, the pull of identification was concentrated on singled-out persons rather than on identifiability in the abstract: a single identified victim drew stronger concern/helping than broader or more statistical targets, supporting the core identifiable-victim pattern.
findings.source_title: The "identified victim" effect: an identified group, or just a single individual?
